question: A 24-year-old woman, who is primiparous, suffers a miscarriage at 7 weeks of gestation. The anatomopathological study of the abortive remains indicates molar disease. We must inform you that:

options.opa: The risk of a new molar gestation in a future pregnancy is 50%.
options.opb: You should not get pregnant until you have regular check-ups and a year of negative beta-HCG levels.
options.opc: No further monitoring is necessary if the evacuation of the trophoblastic tissue was complete.
options.opd: It is necessary to carry out periodic check-ups since in 40% of cases it will develop a gestational trophoblastic neoplasm.

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Molar disease" -> "increased risk of future molar pregnancy" -> "risk not as high as -> 50%
CHAIN: "Molar disease" -> "need for regular check-ups" -> "monitor beta-HCG levels" -> "avoid pregnancy until stable" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Complete evacuation of trophoblastic tissue" -> "possible resolution" -> "risk of complications still present" -> "monitoring recommended" -> 30%
CHAIN: "Molar disease" -> "risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasm" -> "risk not as high as -> 40%
enhanced_information: In cases of molar pregnancy, the risk of recurrence in future pregnancies is increased but not as high as 50%; it is generally around 1-2%. After a molar pregnancy, it is standard to monitor beta-HCG levels until they return to normal to ensure complete resolution and to detect any potential development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). It is recommended to avoid pregnancy until beta-HCG levels have been normal for 6-12 months. Complete evacuation of trophoblastic tissue does not eliminate the need for follow-up, as there is still a risk of GTN, though it is not as high as 40%. Regular follow-up is crucial to monitor for any complications or development of GTN.
analysis: In the case of a molar pregnancy, the risk of recurrence in future pregnancies is increased but not as high as 50%; it is generally around 1-2%. Therefore, option opa is incorrect. After a molar pregnancy, it is crucial to monitor beta-HCG levels until they return to normal to ensure complete resolution and to detect any potential development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN). It is recommended to avoid pregnancy until beta-HCG levels have been normal for 6-12 months, making option opb the most accurate. Option opc is incorrect because even after complete evacuation, follow-up is necessary to monitor for GTN. Option opd is also incorrect because the risk of developing GTN is not as high as 40%. Therefore, the best-supported option is opb, which aligns with standard medical practice of monitoring beta-HCG levels and advising against pregnancy until levels are normal for a specified period.
